content: Testing providers are typically the first to identify issues with diagnostic products, such as misdiagnoses, visual defects, or other anomalies. It is their responsibility to report any adverse events or product problems to national regulatory authorities (NRAs). These authorities often rely on the outcomes of the World Health Organization (WHO) pre-qualification process when evaluating applications for marketing in vitro diagnostic (IVD) products. Manufacturers or their authorized representatives must retain samples of defective test kits and send them back to the manufacturer for root cause analysis. NRAs and reference laboratories should ensure the availability of user feedback forms, such as the WHO user feedback form, which should be simple to use and capture essential details like lot number, expiry date, a description of the issue, and the number of tests and patients affected. Manufacturers are obligated to report adverse events and specific incidents to regulatory authorities as part of their national registration requirements. The regulatory authority will review the manufacturer’s investigation and any corrective actions taken. WHO recommends that manufacturers submit an investigation report to the relevant NRA in cases of serious public health threats or when the use of a medical device results in death, serious health deterioration, or the potential for such outcomes. This includes indirect harm, such as misdiagnosis, delayed diagnosis, delayed treatment, inappropriate treatment, absence of treatment, or transfusion of inappropriate materials. Manufacturers may implement a Field Safety Corrective Action (FSCA) to address product issues by identifying the root cause and taking corrective steps while keeping regulatory authorities informed. An FSCA often involves the return or destruction of the affected product or modifications to the product, such as changes to labeling or instructions for use (IFU). For IVD products recommended by WHO through pre-qualification or emergency use listing, manufacturers must report incidents to WHO. These reports are entered into WHO’s Global Surveillance and Monitoring System for substandard or falsified medical products. WHO oversees the manufacturer’s investigation and any resulting corrective actions or FSCA. If quality issues are not addressed promptly and adequately, the IVD may be removed from the WHO pre-qualified list. WHO also reserves the right to issue Information Notices for Users. The WHO publication Guidance for post-market surveillance and market surveillance of medical devices, including in vitro diagnostics provides further details. Additionally, Annex J of the 2019 HIV Testing Services (HTS) guidelines outlines activities contributing to post-market surveillance. National authorities are encouraged to collaborate with professional External Quality Assessment (EQA) providers to enhance proficiency testing capacity and address issues identified through quality-monitoring activities. EQA is a critical tool for post-market surveillance and identifying testing sites prone to errors that could lead to HIV misdiagnosis. Participation in EQA schemes aims to evaluate testing competence, assess individual provider performance, ensure the reliability of HIV testing procedures, and verify the accuracy of records. Testing sites should participate in EQA schemes as frequently as possible, ideally at least once per year. Annex J of the 2019 HTS guidelines provides additional details on organizing EQA schemes. Accreditation of testing sites involves the recognition of their quality and competence. National accreditation bodies assess whether a testing site complies with quality requirements. The most widely applicable international quality standard is ISO 15189, which outlines requirements for medical laboratories. Authorities should consider moving toward accreditation of testing sites within their tiered testing networks. WHO provides guidance on this process through partnerships. At the testing site level, the principles of a Quality Management System (QMS) must be applied to all services conducting HIV testing and diagnosis. Both facility-based and community-based testing services must ensure quality. Site supervisors are responsible for quality activities and should be trained in QMS principles. Testing services must have a quality policy addressing 12 key aspects, including organization, personnel, equipment, purchasing and inventory, quality control, information management, documentation, occurrence management, assessment, process improvement, client service, and facilities and safety. These aspects are detailed in the WHO Laboratory Quality Stepwise Implementation tool. For HIV self-testing, certain QMS elements, such as organization, personnel, assessment, process improvement, and client service, may not be applicable. Testing services should be organized to suit the community they serve, ensuring accessibility and quality. Quality management should be an ongoing responsibility shared by all staff members, not a one-time activity or the responsibility of a single individual. Testing sites must employ sufficient trained and qualified personnel to handle all phases of the testing process, including preand post-test information, pre-analytical specimen collection and processing, analytical assay procedures, and post-analytical interpretation and reporting of results. Roles and responsibilities must be clearly defined, and all personnel should receive pre-service and in-service training. Regular supportive supervision and mentoring are essential, as is ensuring the psychological and physical well-being of HIV testing providers. Appropriate and fully functional equipment is required for all testing services, regardless of the assay format used. For rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), good lighting, timing devices, and proper storage conditions are critical. For laboratory-based IVDs, equipment calibration and maintenance are essential for accurate results. Testing sites must implement systems to monitor storage conditions and ensure preventive and corrective maintenance of equipment. Stock-outs of HIV test kits or essential consumables can compromise testing quality and outcomes. A system for tracking inventory and monitoring stock levels is necessary to prevent stock-outs and ensure continuous availability of testing supplies. Community-led monitoring systems can help identify and address stock-outs effectively. Quality control (QC) processes must be in place to ensure that testing procedures are performed correctly, environmental conditions are suitable, and assays function as expected. QC aims to detect and address any deviations from expected performance.
